data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI is chiefly a radiative geometry effect: the urban street canyon has a reduced sky view factor, which suppresses longwave radiative cooling to the cold sky after sunset; the cross-city gap scales with building height and built density, which set the effective sky view and therefore the rate of nighttime cooling.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If urban and rural surfaces had identical sky view factors, this mechanism would not produce a nighttime gap.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the nocturnal UHI persisted even when radiative cooling rates were measured to be equal, this mechanism would be overturned.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If flat, low-density cities with high sky view factors exhibited the same UHI intensity as dense skyscraper districts, this mechanism would be weakened.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The fundamental nighttime cooling mechanism is longwave radiative loss to the sky. In the countryside, the surface has an unobstructed view of the cold sky and cools efficiently. In the city, tall buildings block part of the sky hemisphere; surfaces exchange longwave radiation with warmer building walls rather than the cold sky, drastically reducing net radiative cooling. Cities with greater building height and built density have lower sky view factors, so their nighttime cooling is weaker and the UHI gap is more pronounced.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
